title: AI model decodes the language cells use to communicate
key_facts: A team led by Pulin Li (MIT assistant professor of biology, Whitehead Institute member) and graduate student Nicholas Hutchins found each cell signaling pathway leaves a unique gene-activity 'fingerprint'.
The fingerprints are consistent across cell types, so pathways need not be mapped cell type by cell type.
A machine learning model called IRIS detects them and estimates which signals a cell received at different developmental stages, even for unseen cell types.
It was trained on a dataset of thousands of human embryonic stem cells exposed to dozens of combinations of six signaling pathways.
Tested on mouse embryo cells; a model prediction about a pathway promoting lung development was confirmed in mouse embryos.
Published in Nature Methods on 8 Sep; could help stem cell engineering and organoids for studying disease.
quote_evidence: The researchers’ detailed open-access findings, published in the journal Nature Methods on Sept. 8, could accelerate stem cell engineering for regenerative medicine and improve the creation of organoids — miniature, 3D models that mimic real organs — for studying disease mechanisms and testing new drugs.
Experiments in mouse embryos confirmed the model's prediction.
why_it_matters_hint: Could make it cheaper to learn which signals steer stem cells into specific tissues.
